title: Multiplicative MMS guarantee for chores
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
formal: Determine the smallest real \(\alpha \ge 1\) such that, for every finite instance of nonnegative additive chores with any number of agents, there is a complete allocation \((A_{1},\ldots ,A_{n})\) satisfying \(c_{i}(A_{i})\le \alpha \mu _{i}\) for every agent i, where \(\mu _{i}\) is that agent’s minimax share. Denote this universal factor by \(\alpha\)*.
why: Seeks the intrinsic loss required for fair allocation of indivisible burdens.

progress.text: A three-agent, nine-chore example establishes the lower bound \(44/43\).
The scheduling reduction establishes the general upper bound \(13/11\).
Improved ordinal and personalized-bivalued guarantees concern distinct restrictions or benchmarks.
A comparison-query preprint continues to identify \(13/11\) as the general multiplicative frontier.

definitions: An instance has \(n\ge 1\) agents, \(m\ge 0\) indivisible chores, and finite real costs \(c_{i},g\ge 0\). Agent i assigns a bundle \(S\subseteq [m]\) the additive cost \(c_{i}(S)=\sum _{g\in S}c_{i},g\); lower cost is better. Let \(\Pi _{n}([m])\) be the finite set of ordered partitions of \([m]\) into n disjoint bundles, allowing empty bundles. Define \(\mu _{i}=\min _{(\mathrm{P}_{1},\ldots ,\mathrm{P}_{n})\in \Pi _{n}([m])} \max _{1\le j\le n} c_{i}(\mathrm{P}_{j})\). All bundles in this minimum are evaluated using the same agent i’s costs. A complete allocation belongs to \(\Pi _{n}([m])\): each chore has exactly one owner, with no splitting, disposal or payments. The allocation must satisfy all agents’ inequalities simultaneously, although their benchmark partitions can differ. The inequalities also apply when \(\mu _{i}=0\), without dividing by zero; in that case every chore has zero cost to i. There is no computation-time requirement or fixed bound on n or m. The smallest universal factor exists: for each finite instance its feasible factors form a closed upper interval, and the known universal upper bound makes the intersection of these intervals nonempty.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \alpha *|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture.

context_blocks.title: The burden an agent can guarantee herself
context_blocks.text: Imagine partitioning all chores into n bundles before receiving the most costly bundle. The minimax share is the smallest worst burden that the agent can arrange. With two bundles and chore costs 4, 3 and 3, this benchmark is 6, achieved by {4} and \(\{3,3\}\); the proportional cost is only 5. Indivisibility is why the two benchmarks differ.

context_blocks.title: Exact fairness can fail
context_blocks.text: Different agents can disagree about which chores are difficult, so their individually optimal partitions need not fit together. Feige, Sapir and Tauber give a three-agent, nine-chore example in which every agent’s minimax share is 43 but every complete allocation gives someone cost at least 44. Thus \(\alpha *\ge 44/43>1\).

context_blocks.title: The universal gap
context_blocks.text: Huang and Segal-Halevi prove that factor \(13/11\) always suffices. Together with the negative example, the checked bounds are \(44/43\le \alpha *\le 13/11\), approximately 1.0233 to 1.1818. The upper bound is an existence statement at the exact factor; finding such an allocation within a specified running time is an additional question.

context_blocks.title: What newer guarantees cover
context_blocks.text: The 2025 bin-packing paper gives a \(15/13\) multiplicative guarantee for personalized bivalued costs and improves a different, ordinal MMS benchmark in general. These do not replace the general multiplicative bound here. The September 2026 comparison-query preprint still uses \(13/11\) as the general frontier and studies how little preference information an algorithm needs.

context_blocks.title: Why this optimum matters
context_blocks.text: The factor measures the unavoidable loss caused by allocating whole burdens while respecting everyone’s own costs. A factor closer to 1 means that every agent can be kept closer to her personal benchmark. The easy/difficult-chores source gives exact fairness in special cost models, illustrating why those models must be distinguished from unrestricted additive costs.

sentences: Chores are indivisible tasks whose costs add, and each agent prefers a smaller burden.
Her minimax share is the lowest worst-bundle cost she can obtain by partitioning all chores among the agents.
The question asks for the smallest universal factor by which every agent’s share must be relaxed to make a complete allocation possible.
The checked general bounds are \(44/43\) and \(13/11\), while stronger guarantees for restricted costs do not close this gap.
The Lean benchmark accepts a certified determination with absolute error at most 0.01 throughout the stated numerical domain.
